claims.planned: sudo executes a command as another user (default root) according to the sudoers policy; NOPASSWD tag; sudo -l lists what the invoking user may run; env_reset default resets environment
claims.finding: sudo(8): 'allows a permitted user to execute a command as the superuser or another user, as specified by the security policy'; default policy plugin is sudoers (/etc/sudoers). -u picks a target user other than the default (usually root), by name or '#uid'. -l with no command lists the invoking user's privileges on this host. NOPASSWD: a tag on a Cmnd_Spec that removes the authentication requirement for the commands that follow it. env_reset is 'on by default': the command runs in a minimal environment of TERM, PATH, HOME, MAIL, SHELL, LOGNAME, USER and SUDO_* (plus env_keep/env_check matches); PATH is replaced by secure_path if that is set. Executed: caller's FOO, MYTOKEN and custom PATH entry were all absent from `sudo env`; PATH was Ubuntu's secure_path.
claims.quote: sudo allows a permitted user to execute a command as the superuser or another user, as specified by the security policy. The invoking user's real (not effective) user-ID is used to determine the user name with which to query the security policy.

claims.planned: Official minimal images (ubuntu, debian) do not ship sudo — verify by running, not from docs
claims.finding: Verified by running all three course images: sudo is absent from ubuntu:24.04, debian:bookworm-slim and alpine:3.20 (the default user in each is root, uid 0). Invoking it gives the shell's 127 'command not found'. On Ubuntu `apt-get install sudo` provides 1.9.15p5.
claims.quote:
ubuntu:24.04 $ command -v sudo; echo status=$? -> status=1 ; $ sudo true -> sudo: command not found, status=127
debian:bookworm-slim $ sudo true -> sh: 1: sudo: not found, status=127 ; id -> uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
alpine:3.20 $ sudo true -> sh: sudo: not found, status=127

extra_findings.fact: sudo is itself a set-user-ID-root binary, so it cannot work on a nosuid filesystem...
extra_findings.quote: The sudo binary must be owned by the root user and have the set-user-ID bit set. Also, it must not be located on a file system mounted with the 'nosuid' option or on an NFS file system that maps uid 0 to an unprivileged uid.

extra_findings.fact: ...nor under the Linux no_new_privs flag — the manual names containers as the usual cause. This is why `docker run --security-opt no-new-privileges` disables sudo for an agent.
extra_findings.quote: sudo was run by a process that has the Linux "no new privileges" flag is set. This causes the set-user-ID bit to be ignored when running an executable, which will prevent sudo from functioning. The most likely cause for this is running sudo within a container that sets this flag.

$ setpriv --reuid=alice --regid=alice --init-groups --no-new-privs sudo id
sudo: The "no new privileges" flag is set, which prevents sudo from running as root.
sudo: If sudo is running in a container, you may need to adjust the container configuration to disable the flag.
status=1
If no command is specified, list the privileges for the invoking user (or the user specified by the -U option) on the current host.
Run the command as a user other than the default target user (usually root). The user may be either a user name or a numeric user-ID (UID) prefixed with the '#' character (e.g., '#0' for UID 0).

extra_findings.fact: -n (non-interactive): never prompt; fail instead. The right flag for agents and scripts.
extra_findings.quote: Avoid prompting the user for input of any kind. If a password is required for the command to run, sudo will display an error message and exit.

extra_findings.fact: Exit value: the command's own status on success; 1 for authentication failure, configuration/permission problem, or if the command cannot be executed.
extra_findings.quote: Upon successful execution of a command, the exit status from sudo will be the exit status of the program that was executed.
extra_findings.location: sudo(8) EXIT VALUE; executed: sudo bash -c 'exit 42' -> 42

extra_findings.fact: Credential caching: 5 minutes per terminal by default; password prompt timeout 5 minutes.
extra_findings.quote: By default, the sudoers policy caches credentials on a per-terminal basis for 5 minutes.

extra_findings.fact: NOPASSWD exact text and the manual's example.
extra_findings.quote: By default, sudo requires that a user authenticate before running a command. This behavior can be modified via the NOPASSWD tag. ... ray rushmore = NOPASSWD: /bin/kill, /bin/ls, /usr/bin/lprm

extra_findings.fact: A user with any NOPASSWD entry can run `sudo -l` without a password.
extra_findings.quote: By default, if the NOPASSWD tag is applied to any of a user's entries for the current host, the user will be able to run 'sudo -l' without a password.
If set, sudo will run the command in a minimal environment containing the TERM, PATH, HOME, MAIL, SHELL, LOGNAME, USER and SUDO_* variables. ... This flag is on by default.
If set, sudo will use this value in place of the user's PATH environment variable.

extra_findings.fact: Canonical 'anyone in the group may do anything' lines and a blanket NOPASSWD, from the manual's examples.
extra_findings.quote: root ALL = (ALL) ALL / %wheel ALL = (ALL) ALL ... FULLTIMERS ALL = NOPASSWD: ALL

extra_findings.fact: Drop-in files: `@includedir /etc/sudoers.d`, parsed in lexical order. Edit with visudo to avoid syntax errors locking you out.
extra_findings.quote: changes to the configuration files should be made using the visudo(8) utility which will ensure that no syntax errors are introduced.
extra_findings.location: sudo(8) DESCRIPTION; sudoers(5) 'Including other files from within sudoers'

extra_findings.fact: Ubuntu 24.04's stock /etc/sudoers after `apt-get install sudo` (comments stripped); file mode 440 root:root; /usr/bin/sudo is -rwsr-xr-x root root.
extra_findings.quote: Defaults env_reset / Defaults mail_badpass / Defaults secure_path="/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin:/snap/bin" / Defaults use_pty / root ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL / %admin ALL=(ALL) ALL / %sudo ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL / @includedir /etc/sudoers.d

extra_findings.fact: Observed NOPASSWD rule and sudo -l (rule file /etc/sudoers.d/alice, mode 440: 'alice ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/id').
extra_findings.quote:
$ sudo -l -> User alice may run the following commands on <host>: (ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/id
$ sudo id -> uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
$ sudo -u ubuntu id -un -> ubuntu
$ sudo -n cat /etc/shadow -> sudo: a password is required (status 1)
(without -n and no TTY) sudo: a terminal is required to read the password; either use the -S option to read from standard input or configure an askpass helper

extra_findings.fact: Observed env_reset: variables exported by the caller do not reach the command; -E preserves variables but PATH is still secure_path.
extra_findings.quote:
caller: FOO=bar MYTOKEN=abc PATH=/custom/bin:...
$ sudo env | sort -> HOME=/root HOSTNAME=... LANG=C.UTF-8 LOGNAME=root MAIL=/var/mail/root PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin:/snap/bin SHELL=/bin/bash SUDO_COMMAND=/usr/bin/env SUDO_GID=0 SUDO_UID=0 SUDO_USER=root TERM=unknown USER=root
$ sudo -E env | grep -E '^(FOO|MYTOKEN|PATH)=' -> MYTOKEN=abc / FOO=bar / PATH=/usr/local/sbin:...:/snap/bin

extra_findings.fact: In ubuntu:24.04 the preinstalled 'ubuntu' user (uid 1000) is already a member of group sudo, so installing sudo gives that account full sudo rights via the %sudo rule (it has no usable password, so it would still need one set or a NOPASSWD rule).

teaching_notes: Both planned claims hold. The eval-relevant extras: (1) minimal images have no sudo and run as root already, so an agent transcript showing 'sudo: command not found' (127) is an environment fact, not a model failure; (2) sudo is just a setuid-root binary, so nosuid mounts and no_new_privs switch it off, and the manual itself names containers as the usual cause; (3) env_reset + secure_path mean `sudo cmd` does not see the caller's exported variables or PATH additions — a common reason a tool 'works without sudo but not with it'; (4) use `sudo -n` in anything non-interactive so it fails fast instead of hanging on a password prompt. The online manual documents the current upstream release (its exact version was not recorded); Ubuntu 24.04 packages 1.9.15p5.
